overview: Fisher & Paykel Healthcare is a New Zealand-founded (1969) designer, manufacturer and marketer of medical devices used in acute and chronic respiratory care, surgery and the treatment of obstructive sleep apnea (OSA), selling in more than 120 countries. The business is organised into two product groups: Hospital (invasive/noninvasive ventilation, nasal high flow therapy, anesthesia and surgical humidification) and Homecare (OSA masks and home respiratory support). FY2026 (year ended 31 March 2026) operating revenue was NZ$2.31 billion (Hospital ~63%, Homecare ~37%), manufactured in Auckland, New Zealand, Tijuana, Mexico, and a growing Guangzhou, China facility, and dual-listed with its primary quotation on the NZX and a secondary ASX quotation (both ordinary shares in the single NZ-incorporated entity, reported in NZD).

business_model.summary: Classic razor/razorblade model: durable hardware (flow generators, humidifiers, the F&P 950 and Airvo 3 systems) is placed with hospitals and homecare patients, then drives a much larger, recurring stream of single-patient-use consumables (breathing circuits, humidification chambers, OSA masks) that must be replaced regularly. Hospital hardware is roughly 10% of Hospital revenue with consumables ~90%; Homecare hardware is a similar minority share with consumables making up the bulk of Homecare revenue. Growth is driven less by market volume growth and more by actively 'changing clinical practice' — training clinicians to adopt nasal high flow and other therapies as standard of care, which is a multi-year, relationship-driven sales process defensible against low-cost entrants.
business_model.customer_type: B2B — hospitals, healthcare systems and home care/durable medical equipment (DME) providers; end-use by clinicians and patients but purchasing decisions made by institutional and distributor customers
business_model.geographic_mix: FY2026: North America ~48%, Europe ~21%, Asia Pacific ~27%, Other ~4% (approximate, per revenue-by-region disclosure); roughly 99% of operating revenue is generated in currencies other than NZD (USD ~50%, EUR ~19-20%, other ~29%, MXN/NZD ~1% each), while manufacturing costs are substantially NZD- and MXN-denominated, creating a structural revenue/cost currency mismatch that the company only partially hedges

competitive_position.market_position: One of the leading global players in nasal high flow/humidified respiratory therapy (Optiflow/Airvo), with tens of millions of patients treated cumulatively and around 22-24 million patients treated per year across the portfolio; a top-3 global player in OSA/CPAP masks alongside ResMed and Philips, competing on comfort/fit differentiation (F&P Nova, Nova Micro, Vitera, Evora, Solo) rather than scale; company estimates a combined Hospital + Homecare total addressable market of NZ$25bn+ and growing (Hospital 150m+ patients, Homecare 100m+ patients)

moat_factors.description: Nasal high flow therapy adoption is driven by a decade-plus programme of clinical trials, published guidelines and hospital-by-hospital protocol changes (reinforced by a December 2024 JAMA-published randomised trial supporting nasal high flow as a safe alternative to noninvasive ventilation); once embedded into standard of care and hospital purchasing/formulary decisions, switching is slow and costly for competitors to dislodge

A deep global patent portfolio (historically ~900 US patents/applications with a multi-year average remaining life); history of enforcing IP against ResMed (2016-2019 global litigation, settled 2019) demonstrates willingness and capability to defend design moats
Large global installed base of hardware (Airvo/myAirvo systems, flow generators) creates recurring high-margin consumables demand independent of new hardware sales cycles

In-house design, R&D and manufacturing across NZ, Mexico and China supports quality control and a continuous-improvement cost programme, evidenced by over 100bps of constant-currency gross margin improvement in FY2026 despite tariff drag
Multi-decade relationships with intensive care, emergency medicine and sleep clinicians; company positions itself as a trusted clinical partner, not just a device vendor

weaknesses: Sub-scale relative to ResMed and Philips in overall respiratory/sleep device revenue, limiting negotiating leverage with large group purchasing organisations
High revenue concentration in a small number of therapy franchises (Optiflow/nasal high flow, OSA masks) versus more diversified device peers
No major presence in flow generator/CPAP device hardware to rival ResMed's AirSense platform — homecare hardware remains a smaller, lower-margin part of the mix
Heavy USD/EUR revenue vs NZD/MXN cost base structurally exposes reported earnings to FX volatility regardless of hedging
ASX secondary listing has materially thinner liquidity than the NZX primary listing, so local ASX investors may face wider spreads and price discovery that lags NZX

growth_drivers: Continued 'changing clinical practice' campaign expanding nasal high flow (Optiflow) into new applications — emergency department, COPD/GOLD guideline recommendation, post-operative, ICU/HDU and anesthesia use (Optiflow Switch, Optiflow Trace) — supporting consumables growth even in softer hospital admission periods

New OSA mask launches — F&P Nova Nasal (rolled out NZ/Australia, then Europe, then the US) and Nova Micro, alongside Vitera, Evora and Solo ranges, to grow share in the 100m+ patient homecare TAM against ResMed/Philips
F&P 950 System and Airvo 3 hardware roll-out into the United States and other markets driving above-trend hardware growth, which seeds future consumables annuities
Anesthesia product adoption as a newer growth vector within Hospital

Capacity expansion: fifth East Tāmaki (Auckland) building under construction (~NZ$250m cost, targeted operational 2027), a planned second NZ campus at Karaka (plan-change application submitted, decision pending through Auckland Council), continued Tijuana, Mexico expansion and a now fully operational Guangzhou, China manufacturing site (with local China sales commenced) intended to serve China's large market without displacing NZ/Mexico investment

Gross margin recovery programme: continuous improvement initiatives targeting a long-term ~65% constant-currency gross margin (FY2026 actual gross margin above 63%, with further constant-currency improvement guided for FY2027) even while partially absorbing tariff headwinds
R&D intensity (~10-11% of revenue) funding a growing product pipeline across both divisions

Structural demographic tailwinds: aging population and rising prevalence of COPD (an estimated ~400m people worldwide) and other chronic respiratory disease support the Homecare and home respiratory support TAM

US IEEPA tariff refunds (NZ$23m incorporated into FY2027 guidance following the US Supreme Court ruling that IEEPA-based tariffs were unlawful) provide a near-term earnings tailwind and reduce net tariff drag versus FY2026

business.description: Hospital revenue depends partly on respiratory illness admission volumes (flu/RSV/COVID-adjacent seasons); recent periods have grown despite management describing US/major-market respiratory admissions as comparatively subdued or lower-seasonal, but a normalisation or step-down in admissions could pressure consumables growth

ResMed and a post-recall-recovering Philips are both aggressively investing in mask comfort/fit innovation; F&P must continue new product cadence (Nova, Nova Micro, Vitera, Evora, Solo) to defend and grow share

Company explicitly flags product quality/patient safety as a top material risk; a prior product recall provision was large enough to be treated as an abnormal item excluded from underlying NPAT comparisons in FY2024
History of costly multi-year global patent litigation with ResMed (2016-2019, settled); respiratory/OSA device IP remains contested territory industry-wide

financial.risk: FX mismatch between revenue and cost base
financial.description: Roughly 99% of operating revenue is non-NZD (USD ~50%, EUR ~19-20%) while a substantial share of costs are NZD/MXN-denominated and profit is reported in NZD; despite a multi-year hedging programme, spot/hedge-rate movement can swing reported net profit by tens of millions of NZ dollars even in a strong operating year, and hedge cover thins in the outer years of the programme

Capex (including land/buildings, plant/equipment, intangibles) has stepped up materially, driven by the fifth East Tāmaki building and the Karaka land parcel (with a final payment due), a multi-year step-up versus the historical run-rate that pressures free cash flow before the new capacity generates revenue

financial.risk: Dividend payout growth outpacing near-term FCF
financial.description: Dividends grew strongly in FY2026 (total dividend up ~22%) against solid but capex-constrained free cash flow — currently well covered given the company's net cash position, but the capex step-up and suspended dividend reinvestment plan reduce the cash-flow buffer

regulatory.description: US tariffs have been a recurring constant-currency gross margin drag on hospital products sourced from New Zealand and Mexico; while a Supreme Court ruling on IEEPA tariffs generated a one-off NZ$23m refund incorporated into FY2027 guidance, the broader US tariff policy environment remains fluid and a source of ongoing cost and forecasting uncertainty

regulatory.risk: NZ Medical Products Bill / Patents Amendment Bill
regulatory.description: Company actively engages with NZ's Ministry of Health and Parliament on proposed legislation that could alter the domestic regulatory and IP environment for its core manufacturing base

Market access depends on maintaining product licences (FDA, EU MDR, China NMPA and others) across 120+ countries; regulatory delays can slow new product launches such as the staggered US/Europe/APAC rollout of Nova Nasal

As a foreign-exempt/dual-listed entity on ASX with its home exchange being NZX, FPH must satisfy both regulators' continuous disclosure regimes, adding modest incremental compliance overhead versus a single-market listing

macro.risk: NZD/USD and NZD/EUR exchange rate volatility
macro.description: The single largest identified swing factor in reported (vs constant-currency) earnings; a stronger NZD compresses reported margins and profit even when underlying constant-currency performance is strong — and for ASX investors, AUD/NZD cross-rate movements add a further layer of currency translation on top of the underlying NZD result
Company disclosures cite ongoing trade tensions, tariffs and geopolitical conflict as reinforcing the importance of resilient, geographically diversified supply chains (NZ + Mexico + China)

macro.risk: Freight, resin and input cost inflation
macro.description: Petrochemical-derived resin, packaging and global freight are meaningful cost of sales inputs; company climate/macro disclosures flag shipping/freight and resin cost inflation risk
Hospital capital equipment purchases (hardware) can be deferred in tighter public/private hospital budget environments even though consumables demand is comparatively resilient

macro_factors.industry_outlook: Global respiratory care and OSA device markets continue to grow on aging demographics, rising chronic respiratory disease prevalence (COPD affects an estimated ~400m people worldwide) and continued clinical guideline support for nasal high flow therapy; company estimates a combined Hospital + Homecare addressable market of NZ$25bn+ and growing
macro_factors.cyclicality: Moderate — Hospital hardware sales have some capex cyclicality tied to hospital budgets, but the large consumables base (the majority of both Hospital and Homecare revenue) is recurring and relatively defensive; COVID-19 (FY2021-22) caused a sharp hardware demand pull-forward followed by a multi-year consumables/utilisation normalisation that has now largely worked through the base, with recent hardware growth again running well ahead of consumables, suggesting a fresh, organic (not COVID-related) hardware upgrade cycle
macro_factors.interest_rate_sensitivity: Low direct sensitivity (net cash position, minimal debt), but higher rates raise the discount rate applied to FPH's premium growth-stock multiple and increase relative attractiveness of yield alternatives on both the NZX and ASX
key_input_costs: US import tariffs on NZ- and Mexico-sourced hospital product

recent_developments.event: Company provided H1 FY2027 guidance and raised full-year FY2027 guidance: operating revenue now expected at NZ$2.47-2.57bn (up from NZ$2.45-2.57bn) and NPAT at NZ$525-565m (up from NZ$500-550m), incorporating NZ$23m of US IEEPA tariff refunds following the US Supreme Court ruling that Trump-administration IEEPA tariffs were unlawful; H1 FY2027 (to 30 Sept 2026) guided at ~NZ$1.24bn revenue (+14%) and ~NZ$280m NPAT (+24% excluding tariff refunds)

FY2026 annual results announced: operating revenue NZ$2.31bn (+14% reported, +12% constant currency), NPAT NZ$468.5m (+24% reported), gross margin improved despite ~90bps of US tariff drag, total dividend up 22% for the year; results were broadly in line with analyst revenue forecasts and about 2% ahead on NPAT (per Jefferies commentary); FY2027 initial guidance issued of operating revenue NZ$2.45-2.57bn and NPAT NZ$500-550m
Company upgraded FY2026 guidance mid-year: operating revenue raised to ~NZ$2.30bn and NPAT raised to ~NZ$450-470m, reflecting stronger-than-expected hospital hardware and consumables demand

H1 FY2026 (six months to 30 Sep 2025) results: operating revenue surpassed NZ$1bn for the first half for the first time, at NZ$1.09bn (+14% reported, +12% constant currency); NPAT NZ$213.0m (+39% reported, +28% constant currency); gross margin 63.0% (+110bps reported, +60bps constant currency, including a US tariff impact); interim dividend raised to 19.0 cps from 18.5 cps
F&P Nova Nasal OSA mask progressively launched in Europe and then the United States, following earlier launches in New Zealand and Australia

Construction progressed on the fifth East Tāmaki, Auckland manufacturing/R&D building (~NZ$250m, targeted operational 2027); plan-change application for the second Karaka, Auckland campus continued through Auckland Council review; Guangzhou, China manufacturing facility became fully operational with local China sales commencing

US tariff policy (including on Mexico- and NZ-sourced hospital products) increased FPH's cost base through FY2026, before a portion was subsequently refunded in FY2027 following the IEEPA court ruling

guidance.as_of: H1 FY2027 Guidance Update, 21 August 2026 (supersedes FY2027 guidance issued with FY2026 annual results on 26 May 2026)

items.notes: Raised from initial FY2027 guidance of NZ$2.45-2.57bn issued 26 May 2026; implies continued double-digit growth over FY2026's NZ$2.31bn
Raised from initial FY2027 guidance of NZ$500-550m; incorporates NZ$23m of US IEEPA tariff refunds; implies growth over FY2026's NZ$468.5m
Implies ~14% growth over H1 FY2026's NZ$1.09bn
Implies ~24% growth over H1 FY2026's NZ$213.0m excluding tariff refunds; includes a portion of the NZ$23m IEEPA refund

items.target: Continued overall improvement in constant currency
items.notes: Company continues to target a longer-term structural gross margin around 65% in constant currency; guidance assumes current global tariff rates, policies and applications continue for the remainder of FY2027

items.target: No single explicit FY2027 figure disclosed in guidance updates; historical run-rate has stepped up materially versus pre-FY2025 levels
items.notes: Continued spend expected on the fifth East Tāmaki building (targeted operational 2027) and the Karaka land payments

guidance.management_commentary: CEO Lewis Gradon highlighted continued strong demand for the company's latest hardware devices (F&P Airvo 3, F&P 950 System) and ongoing change in clinical practice driving consumables sales as the key growth engines into FY2027, describing a strong start to H1 driven particularly by the Hospital product group. Management has repeatedly framed growth as being driven more by clinical-practice change and new-applications adoption than by hospital admission cyclicality, noting strong Hospital consumables growth even in periods of comparatively subdued or lower-seasonal respiratory hospital admissions. The company reiterated its commitment to reaching a ~65% constant-currency gross margin target and continues to apply 'long-term thinking' to navigating US tariff policy, in consultation with NZ government trade officials.

bull_case: Durable razor/razorblade economics: the large majority of both Hospital and Homecare revenue is recurring consumables riding on a large and still-growing global hardware installed base, giving high revenue visibility and pricing power

Structural, multi-decade 'changing clinical practice' growth engine (new nasal high flow guidelines, new applications in ED/COPD/anesthesia/ICU) that has proven durable even against softer hospital admission cycles

Clear, credible path to margin expansion: constant-currency gross margin has improved for multiple consecutive years toward a ~65% long-term target, with FY2027 guided to further improvement and a one-off US tariff refund tailwind

Strong balance sheet and cash generation (net cash position, minimal debt) funding the capex supercycle (fifth East Tāmaki building, Karaka campus, Mexico/China expansion) without needing to raise capital

Geographically diversified, in-house manufacturing (NZ, Mexico, now fully operational China facility) plus a deep patent portfolio provide resilience against single-country tariff or supply-chain shocks and defend against low-cost competitors
FY2027 guidance has already been raised once (August 2026), signalling positive momentum and management's willingness to upgrade mid-cycle
bear_case: Persistently premium valuation (one of the largest companies on the NZX, also ASX-listed) prices in years of above-market growth and margin recovery; any growth disappointment or delay in reaching the ~65% gross margin target risks a de-rating independent of underlying operating performance

Structural NZD-cost/USD-EUR-revenue mismatch means reported earnings and margins remain hostage to currency moves regardless of operational execution, and ASX investors bear an additional layer of AUD/NZD cross-rate translation risk on top of the underlying NZD result

US tariff policy remains an unpredictable, only partially and unevenly mitigated cost and political risk — the IEEPA refund is a one-off benefit, not a guarantee against future tariff actions, given the company's meaningfully NZ- and Mexico-sourced manufacturing base

Heavy capex step-up (fifth East Tāmaki building, second Karaka campus, Mexico/China capacity) suppresses free cash flow conversion over the next several years before new capacity translates into incremental revenue, and land/construction cost overruns are a real execution risk

Competitive intensity from ResMed and a post-recall-recovering Philips Respironics in OSA masks, plus Vyaire/Getinge/Draeger in hospital respiratory, could compress FPH's share gains or force higher R&D/marketing spend to sustain new product cadence
ASX secondary-listing liquidity is thinner than the NZX primary listing, which can mean wider bid/ask spreads and price discovery that lags the home market for ASX-based investors
